name: Fintan, son of NIALL Nioganach

attributes.attribute: ate hazel nuts in a river pool
queen who brought women to Ireland
tale where the son of Niall appears

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Fintan means the white ancient. Several important figures wore this name. Fintan the salmon swam in a pool at the source of an Irish river. The pool lay sometimes on the Boyne, sometimes on the Erne. He fed on hazel nuts that fell from magical bushes. The druid Finneces caught him, and the hero Fionn mac Cumhaill ate him by accident, gaining great wisdom. Fintan mac Bochra was the most ancient of Irishmen. He alone survived the flood that carried the queen Cesair and fifty women to Ireland. Only three men came with the women, and two of them perished of embraces. Fintan fled and changed into many shapes, becoming a one-eyed salmon, an eagle, and a hawk. Amairgin and Tuan Mac Cairill, both bards, show the same power, as do several divinities. By contrast, Fintan, son of Niall Nioganach, takes a small role in the story Intoxication of the Ulstermen.

okr.objective: Fintan is a name shared by several figures across Irish legend.
key_results: Fintan the salmon was eaten by Fionn mac Cumhaill.
Fintan mac Bochra survived the great flood.
Fintan, son of Niall Nioganach, appears in the Intoxication of the Ulstermen.
